ed-berry-shawnee-1915-08-06.A1:
MOB HANGS NEGRO TO TELEPHONE POLE
Oklahoma Victim Admits Guilt to Criminal Assault on White Women.
Shawnee, Okla., Aug. 6.—Ed Berry, negro, charged with two cases of criminal assault and suspected in connection with ten others that have occurred here in the last three years, was taken from officers early today and hanged to a telephone pole at the scene of one of his alleged crimes.

Berry was secretly brought here for trial from the penitentiary at McAlester. When the train arrived and the deputy sheriff and his prisoner alighted, they were covered by revolvers in the hands of a dozen masked men. The officer was disarmed. Ten or twelve automobiles filled with masked men then appeared and the negro was quickly to the Beard street bridge.

When the rope was adjusted around Berry's neck, he was question about the crimes and asked if he were guilty. In each instance he nodded his head affirmatively. In every case the negro's victim was a white woman.

Following the confession the negro was hanged in the presence of about 75 men, all masked, after which the crowd dispersed.

After daylight the body of the negro was cut down and removed to an undertaking establishment. An inquest will be held. Since July 11 berry had been carried from one place to another and finally lodged in the penitentiary at McAlester for safe keeping it being feared, because of the general indignation over what was said to be the delay in bringing the negro to trial, that he would be lynched. Berry's case was to have been heard August 9.
ed-berry-shawnee-1915-08-06.A9:
SLAYER IS
LYNCHED
By United Press.
By United Press.
Shawnee, Aug. 6.—Ed Berry was lynched here today by a mob of enraged citizens after an alleged confession that he had killed two women and attacked many more. He was taken from officers and hanged to a tree close to where his last crime was committed.
Feeling is running high high among citizens here, the whole community being deeply stirred. No arrests followed the lynching. It is unknown yet what action will will follow.
ed-berry-shawnee-1915-08-06.A10:
ADMITTED HAD ATTACKED
MORE THAN SCORE WOMEN
CHARGED WITH MURDER OF TWO WOMEN
Special to The Daily Leader.

Special to The Daily Leader.

Shawnee, Okla., Aug. 6.—Ed Berry, notorious negro, charged with the commission of numerous atrocious crimes, was taken from the officers by an orderly crowd of determined citizens this morning and lynched.

The mob took the negro to the scene of his latest crime and hung him to a tree.

Just before he was strung up, the negro admitted that he had killed the two women for which he was arrested and boasted that he had also made attacks on twenty other women.

Berry was a bad man and had a reputation for killing before coming to Pottawatomie county.

It is now quite certain that it was he who killed two women found dead in a field here some months ago.

When the mob approached the jail they demanded the negro; the sheriff refused and the mob rushed him. Not a shot was fired or an unnecessary word spoken.

The members of the mob were quietly determined and executed the negro without demonstration.

A written confession, it is said was secured from the negro, before he was lynched.
ed-berry-shawnee-1915-08-06.A11:
Women See Executions and Crowd Sings Hymn-One Slayer Pursued.
MEMPHIS, Aug. 7.—Nine negroes were hanged, seven legally and two lynched, yesterday, in the southern states, while a tenth is being chased near Liberty, Mo., by a lynching party.

Alabama led the list with four legal hangings. The governor refused reprieves in each case. At Evergreen, Robert Watkins and John Salter were hanged while a squad of militiamen stood guard to prevent disorder, threatened by citizens who wanted the blacks burned for the murder and assault of Mrs. Mary Lassiter at Cullman.

George James was hanged for the murder of George Clayburn, who was shot through an open window while he was reading a Bible. Millard Carpenter was hanged at Birmingham for the murder two years ago of John T. Camp, a white man.

WOMEN ATTEND HANGING.

Mississippi hanged three negroes, but with two of them, Peter Bolen and Jim Seales, convicted of murdering another negro, an unusual spectacle was made. The hanging was at Fresco, the gallows being erected between two beautiful hills in a natural amphitheater.

Many women were in the crowd of 5,000 people and excursions were run from nearby towns. Just as the traps were sprung simultaneously the crowd burst forth into the hymn, "There Is a Land of Pure Delight," at the request of the negroes just before death.

Bunyan Walters was hanged at Fayetteville, Miss., for the murder of Tom Neals.

AN "ORDERLY MOB."

Dispatches from Shawnee, Okla., tell of a "quiet, orderly crowd armed to the teeth," which hanged Ed Berry to a Santa Fe railroad bridge, riddled his body with bullets and dispersed in as orderly a fashion as it had formed.

In the early morning hours at Trilby, Fla., a crowd, hypnotized with fury, lynched Will Leach, accused of attacking a 13-year-old girl.

At last reports a mob of 500 men were closing in on a negro near Liberty, Mo., who attacked a farmer's wife. Lynching is almost certain, it is said.
ed-berry-shawnee-1915-08-06.A21:
NEGRO IS LYNCHED BY PARTIES UNKNOWN
Special to The World. SHAWNEE OKI
SHAWNEE, Okla., Aug. 6.—A coroner's jury in session here Friday afternoon declared that Ed Berry, the negro who was lynched by a mob Friday morning, came to his death at the hands of a mob composed of parties unknown to the jury. Berry's body still is unclaimed in a local undertaking establishment.

Berry was accused of having committed a criminal assault upon a white woman during the night of July 11. A mutilated half-dollar taken at the time of the assault led to Berry's arrest.

ed-berry-shawnee-1915-08-06.A25:
NEGRO CHURCH IS DYNAMITED
Wellton Startled by Night Explosion Coming As Aftermath of Lynching at Shawnee
WELLSTON, Aug. 9.—Coming as an echo of the lynching of the negro ravisher Ed Berry at Shawnee, Friday, unknown persons Saturday night exploded a stick of dynamite under the negro church at this place. The explosion aroused the town and damaged the building to considerable extent, tearing off some siding and splintering a section of the floor about twelve feet square. As yet no clue as to the identity of the dynamiter has been secured. Throughout this region there is considerable race feeling as the result of Ed Berry's confessions and his lynching at the hands of a mob.

ed-berry-shawnee-1915-08-06.A33:
"BIG BALLOONS—DEAD DUCKS."
Mommouth, Ills., Aug. 14, 1915.
Editor Gazette, Dear Sir;—When I received my paper, Saturday morning, Aug. 14, 1915, I turned to the editorial page and the first thing I saw was the heading "A Speedy Civil Rights Victory," thought how proud our people of Ohio should be of the work you have done for the race, especially while you were a member of the Ohio legislature. Your "Civil Rights" law and your "Anti-lynchery" law have made it possible for our people of Ohio not to be discriminated against without one being made to suffer for it. You are doing more for the betterment of our people of Ohio than the ministers of your city and the state of Ohio should encourage their congregations to take The Gazette.
"Every Colored person who takes and reads it will find that he is carrying a weapon of protection against discrimination in all public places. If there is any race in the race of your people of Ohio, the Gazette, just consider them big hoops filled with poor gas; but them in the class with dead ducks—not worthy to be shot at.

"I shall see our ministers of Monmouth and ask them to encourage the people to take the paper and mention what you have accomplished for our people especially while a member of the state legislature of Ohio.

AN UNCIVILIZED STATE.

The south is indulging in a veritable orgy of hangings. Ten in one day is a recent record, a record that it is to be hoped will stand for all time. Alabama, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Florida contributed. Of the ten hangings, all the victims being Negroes, four in Alabama and three in Mississippi were legal. The remaining three were not. Oklahoma and Florida were lynchings, Vicious and degrading as are lynchings, it is doubtful if the crimes committed in Florida and Oklahoma were more destructive of civilization than the legal hanging of two offenders in Mississippi. The execution was converted into a sort of Roman holiday. The gallows were erected between two hills forming a natural amphitheater accommodating thousands. Here gathered men, women and children to witness the spectacle. There were refreshment stands, Politicians prosecuted their own camp, and the enforcement of the law in its sternest aspect was converted into a debasing and brutalizing jubilee. Mississippi is in need of civilization—Cleveland Plain Dealer.

CORONER UNABLE TO GET EVIDENCE AGAINST MOBMEN AT M'GEHEE'S One of Negroes Left For Dead May Live and Give Testimony
The coroner's investigation of the killing at McGehee's Switch Wednesday morning, when two negroes were shot to death and a third dangerously wounded, adjourned yesterday after hearing five witnesses, and will be resumed when Ed. Russell, the negro left for dead by the mob, is sufficiently recovered to give testimony.

Russell, wounded by five bullets, lies at a local hospital in a dangerous condition. It is thought that he will live, and the strength of the investigation depends on his recovery, since through him the authorities hope to learn the identity of those who composed the mob. No one is allowed to see the negro.

No New Details.

No new details were uncovered by the officials yesterday to throw light on the identity of those in the lynching party. All sources of information stated that it was composed of four white men who drove to the Crenshaws plantation; forced the negroes to come from their homes, and carried them away.

A short time later, and between three and four o'clock in the morning, pistol shots awakened Ed. Crenshaw, whose home is on the plantation. A searching party was organized, and later found the bodies of the three negroes.

Bodies in Ditch.

The bodies were found in a ditch at the side of the road. Harry Russell and Kit Jackson were dead. Ed. Russell, dangerously wounded, lay beside them, where the mob had left him for dead. The wounded negro was rushed to Montgomery by Sheriff Waller at five o'clock in the morning.

The three men lynched were under bond at the county jail, following their arrest last June on the charge of poisoning horses on the plantation of Dr. McLean, where the negroes were living at that time. Alex Jackson, a fourth negro charged with this offense, still remains in the county jail. The case against the four has been continued from time to time in the city court, and never has been brought to trial.

Although the four men in the lynching party are said to have been unmasked, no one has been found to give further clue to their identity than that they were white. In the darkness of the early morning it is considered that complete identification is virtually impossible, unless it was revealed by them to the three negroes who were intended to be their victims, and were considered by them as dead men who could never tell. That one of these negroes lived is considered by authorities to be the one thing that may bring the mobmen into the hands of the law.

Work Is Careful.

The work of these men, in spite of its boldness, was careful, according to testimony given at the coroner's inquest yesterday morning. Coming to the house of one negro which was located at a convenient point they forced its occupant to guide them to the homes of the negroes for whom they were searching. Lights, even a match to light a cigarette, were not permitted. Care was taken that no faces should be seen, and silence was enforced by revolvers.

Kit Jackson was taken from his home, and his hands tied behind him. Ed. and Harry Russell were taken in the same way, and all forced to get in the automobile which stood in the road. The car was turned back toward Montgomery, and a short distance from where it started the bodies of the negroes were found.

Thirteen shots took effect in the three bodies. Kit Jackson was shot three times, in the abdomen, the chest and the right arm. Harry Russell received bullets in his head, stomach, side, groin and face. Ed. Russell, who survived, received five bullet wounds.
henry-russell-hope-hull-1915-08-18.A6:
VIOLENCE BEGETTING VIOLENCE.
tute Alabama for Georgia, in view of the lynching in Montgomery county?

INQUIRER.

We should if we were accustomed to shut our eyes to the truth and to think loosely and lightly. Because four men in Alabama perpetrate a crime does not excuse the continued record of Georgia in violence. If Alabama's record for lynching and for violence was quite as bad as Georgia's, there would still be no excuse for palliating a criticism of the repeated acts of violence perpetrated in Georgia, for which no one has been punished.

In Alabama lynching is rare and sporadic; in Georgia, it is apparently habitual.

Georgia leads all States in the Union in lynchings; it furnished sixteen per cent of the total of the lynchings in the past year. It has for years past led other States in acts of violence. It is the only State in the Union which ever supplied a mob to lynch the Governor. It is the State in which twenty-five negroes were shot down on the streets of Atlanta. It is the State in which a prisoner, supposedly under the protecting aegis of the law, behind the shield and buckler of the law first had his throat cut in prison, and was then turned over to a mob of less than thirty men to be carried more than a hundred miles to be hanged.

Any sins of omission or commission by Alabama does not wipe out that record, and the man who thinks Alabama is estopped from criticising Georgia because four men kill two negroes is a light thinker with a splendid indifference to facts and logic.

Nor can Georgia's record be set up in extenuation of the crime in Alabama. Four men can hardly be called a mob. The offense they committed was fully equal to that of a lynching mob, but it was an outbreak of neighborhood feud, in which four men replied to one crime with another.

The Advertiser's friend, Mr. Alva Fitzpatrick, in another column, takes exception to the statement of The Advertiser, "It is the bloody record of Georgia in violence which has revealed the true character of its ruling class." and commenting on this he says:

After all, it was the highest exponent of Georgia's "ruling class" in the person of Governor Slaton whose executive act in conservation of official duty, that provoked the shocking crime which prompted the Georgia mob into its riot of outrage and crime. But this mob, considerable in number and diabolical in spirit, as it was, is neither the ruling class, nor a majority of the people of Georgia—a fact which appears to have escaped differentiation in your conclusion that calls for the destruction of the State of Georgia and the expose in character of blood, of the "ruling class" of Georgia.

Our correspondent forgets that, even though John M. Slaton had been elected Governor of Georgia, the representative of the "ruling class" marched out to lynch him for the commission of an official act. He forgets that John M. Slaton is today an exile from Georgia—a man whose life is in danger should he return to Georgia. A representative of the "ruling class," several times elected to the highest office in the Capital City of the State, Mayor James H. Woodward, in San Francisco, extolled the lynching of Frank and warned Governor Slaton not to return to Georgia "within a year—if then."

Certainly, less than thirty men, forming the mob which lynched Frank do not form a majority of the citizens of Georgia, but they may be properly recognized as representatives of the ruling class, when, without fear of the consequences, they can tear aside the protection of the law thrown around a prisoner, break open a State prison, rush a prisoner half across the State and lynch him in open daylight. When they can do this in contempt of the law, we may well regard them as representative of the majority sentiment of Georgia.

Why confine the discussion of Georgia's record for violence to the Frank case? The Advertiser, in the article of which our correspondent complained, said specifically:

It was not the lynching of Leo Frank which tore the mask of hypocrisy from this smug declaration; it was not the pusillanimous administration of the criminal law, which weakly failed to protect a prisoner within the keeping of the law, whose life had been continually threatened, which revealed its insincerity. It was not the glaring negligence of the officers, charged with the administration of the law, who allowed a weak and helpless prisoner to have his throat cut, which showed up its hypocrisy. It was not even the civic crime revealed in an open attempt to lynch the Governor of Georgia, which proved that mob violence in that State was fostered and protected.

It is not this one case which drew the comment, it is the repeated acts of violence in Georgia, with the connivance of the representatives of the law, which inspired that comment. Have the members of the mob which went to the home of Governor Slaton and tried to lynch him been punished? Will the members of the mob that perpetrated the violence of the State farm and lynched Frank be punished? Have the members of mob after mob in Georgia been punished, or have any of the officers of the law who truckled to them and helped them been removed from office?

We see in our criticism of mob violence "no provocation for a Southern man to wince under." We do not propose to apologize for mob violence, or to excuse lynching and violence, as pardonable expression of the high spirits of Southern men. Northern papers may present lynching and violence as favorite Southern pastimes; The Advertiser will certainly not assist them in preaching this wrong to the South.

We feel justified in alluding to The Advertiser's prediction that violence would beget violence. On Tuesday afternoon a negro was lynched in Bainbridge, Ga. During the same night two negroes were shot by four white men in Montgomery county. The first newspaper account of the double killing in which automobiles were used read:

"The use of automobiles for the purpose was inspired by the success attained by those who lynched Frank, and it can be said that the Montgomery county lynching was really caused by the Frank lynching."
henry-russell-hope-hull-1915-08-18.A11:
NO NEW EVIDENCE FOUND BY SHERIFF OF HOPE HULL MOB Ed Russell, Negro Left For Dead at Lynching, Carefully Guarded at Hospital
A delay of at least several days will be caused in the investigation by the Sheriff's office and a Coroner's jury of the lynching of two negroes Wednesday morning at Hope Hull, due to the high excitement which prevails among the negroes of that section, and to the serious condition of Ed Russell, the negro dangerously shot by the mobsmen when the other two were killed.

A guard is being maintained at the hospital over the wounded negro in anticipation of a possible attack by one of the four white men who composed the mob. His story of the lynching remains untold, entrance to his room being denied to all but officers and hospital attendants.

It is from Russell that the authorities hope to learn the identity of the men in the mob. He is suffering from a broken hip, and four other bullet wounds. His condition is said to be such as to make questioning inadvisable at present.

It was declared at the Sheriff's office yesterday that practically no information concerning the actual lynching could be obtained, the negroes who know being fearful of death for themselves at the hands of a mob if they divulge their secret.

The present intention of the authorities is to cease questioning for several days that the tension may be relieved, and that those who may be able to throw light on the killing may recover their nerve.

A general exodus of negroes from the vicinity of the lynching is predicted by persons acquainted with conditions there. It is declared that they are living in mortal fear that they, too, may be called from their homes, tied and shot.

Speculation was rife yesterday concerning the identity of the four members of the mob. The names of several persons were spoken freely in this connection. So far as is known no evidence has been unearthed connecting any of the persons mentioned with the crime.
henry-russell-hope-hull-1915-08-18.A12:
Government by Law, or "Clan"? "Government by Law, or "Clan"?
"Clansmen" are active now in Alabama. Early Wednesday morning, within ten miles of Montgomery, the capital of the state and a thriving city, three negro men, under a charge of poisoning mules, were lynched. The "clansmen," it is stated, "proceeded quickly." No noisy fellows they. "They went to the men's homes, bound and gagged them, riddled their bodies with bullets and threw them into a ditch.

The negroes had been in jail in Montgomery awaiting trial, but the day before had been released on bonds and had returned to their homes. "This action," according to the story, "infuriated the white farmers," and the lynching followed.

Let it be noted that the negroes, although under such a grave charge, had been able to furnish bonds, which should go to their credit; that those bonds had been accepted by white men in authority, as all officials in Alabama are white; and that upon being released from prison the negroes had returned to the scene of their accusation, which also should go to their credit. Guilty men of their color would probably have gone elsewhere.

The law was lynched along with the three negroes. Had they remained in jail they might have escaped death. But when the officials at Montgomery accepted bonds—a duty under the law for them to do—the "clansmen" became "infuriated" and took matters into their own hands.

While the country was in a state of hysteria over the lynching of Leo Frank and the headlines of the daily papers were bold and black and their columns crowded with every detail of that awful affair, the following modest despatch of three lines from Montgomery, Ala., appeared in an equally modest place in several papers; some failed to record it:

MONTGOMERY, Ala., Aug. 18.—Three negroes, recently released from jail, where they were held charged with poisoning mules, were lynched near Hopehull early to-day.

Three Negroes lynched on the charge of having poisoned some mules, and that after they had been released from jail! But, perhaps, this little affair was pulled off in Alabama just to divert the attention of the country or to somewhat relieve the strain. Yet, if that was the purpose, it was a miserable failure, for the lynching of the three Negroes attracted no wider attention than did the original offense of poisoning the mules.

KENTUCKY RACE WAR FEARED Night Riders Whip White and Black Men and Women to Drive Out Negroes.
Lexington, Ky., Aug. 19.—Two counties in Western Kentucky—Christian and Caldwell—are reported to be on the verge of a race war as the result of outrages by gangs of night riders. Several men and women were whipped with switches this week. All negroes have been ordered to leave the affected sections on pain of death.

Some are flocking to safe counties or over the state line into Indiana. In other places negroes have armed themselves, it is stated, and defy the night riders, declaring that they will not be driven out, as some of them own their homes.

In a raid at Wynn post office a white man and a negro woman were beaten almost to death. Every negro there was ordered to go away on pain of death. Two white men also warned fled.

At Princeton, J. K. McGoodwin, father of Preston Goodwin, United States minister to Venezuela, received a warning note tied in switches, ordering him to discharge all his negro employes or be hanged. He discharged them.

Trouble seems caused by the fact that many negroes have been employed where white men formerly were. So far the state authorities have taken no action.

Night Riders in Kentucky. Are Again Becoming Active Are Again Becoming Active
NASHVILLE. Tenn., Aug. 19.—Night riders have become active in Caldwell and Christian counties, Kentucky, according to advices received here from Princeton and Hopkinsville today. In the northern part of Christian county fifteen men, masked and armed, went to homes of white and negro people. Several persons were whipped. Notices were left for the residents to move from the community.

At Princeton a warning note and a bundle of thorn switches were left at the brickyard of J. K. McGoodwin, and as a result of the threat McGoodwin has discharged his negro laborers. Mr. McGoodwin is the father of Preston B. McGoodwin, minister to Venezuela.
